decks.title: Motion — Part 1: Displacement, velocity, acceleration and motion graphs
goals: Distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity, and give their SI units
Define average and instantaneous velocity and acceleration
Plot and read position–time and velocity–time graphs, using slope and area
Find average velocity and displacement from graphs

slides.heading: Motion
slides.body_md: Part 1: how we describe where a body is, how fast it goes and how its motion changes, in words, numbers and graphs.

visual.alt: Table of the main quantities used to describe motion, their symbols, SI units and whether they are scalars or vectors

slides.narration: Everything around us moves. A cyclist on a ghat road, a train leaving a station, a ceiling fan, even the Moon. To describe motion in a clear way, physicists use a few careful words: distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. In this part we meet each one, learn its unit, and then see how a graph can show the whole story of a journey at a glance.

slides.heading: Distance and displacement
slides.body_md: **Distance** is the total length of the path travelled. It has only size, so it is a **scalar**. **Displacement** is the shortest straight-line change of position from the start to the end, with its direction. It is a **vector**. Both are measured in metres (m) in the SI system. Distance is never negative and never decreases; displacement can be smaller than the distance, and it can even be zero.

slides.narration: Imagine walking from home to school by a road that goes east and then turns north. The distance is the length of the whole road you walked. The displacement is the straight arrow from your home to the school, with a direction. Distance has size only, so it is a scalar. Displacement has size and direction, so it is a vector. Both are measured in metres.

slides.heading: Speed and velocity
slides.body_md: **Speed** is the distance covered per unit time: $\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. **Velocity** is the displacement per unit time: $\text{velocity} = \dfrac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}}$. The SI unit of both is metre per second (m s⁻¹). To change km/h to m/s, multiply by $\dfrac{1000}{3600} = \dfrac{1}{3.6}$.

rows: Never negative, never zero while moving
Can be positive, negative or zero

visual.alt: Table comparing speed and velocity

slides.narration: Speed tells us how fast a body moves, so it uses distance divided by time. Velocity uses displacement divided by time, so it also tells us the direction. Both are measured in metres per second. A speedometer shows speed only, because it cannot tell you the direction. To change kilometres per hour to metres per second, divide by three point six.

slides.heading: Worked example: distance, displacement, speed, velocity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Ravi cycles 600 m east and then 800 m north. The whole trip takes 600 s (10 minutes). Find the distance, the displacement, the average speed and the average velocity.

**Step 1: distance** $= 600 + 800 = 1400$ m.

**Step 2: displacement.** The two legs are at right angles, so $\sqrt{600^2 + 800^2} = 1000$ m, at about 53° north of east.

**Step 3: average speed** $= 1400 / 600 \approx 2.3$ m s⁻¹.

**Step 4: average velocity** $= 1000 / 600 \approx 1.7$ m s⁻¹ in the direction of the displacement.

visual.alt: Worked table for the cyclist: distance 1400 metres, displacement 1000 metres, average speed 2.3 metres per second and average velocity 1.7 metres per second

slides.narration: Let us work it step by step. The path length is the sum of the two legs, fourteen hundred metres. The legs are at right angles, so the displacement follows from the Pythagoras rule and comes to one thousand metres. Dividing the distance by six hundred seconds gives the average speed. Dividing the displacement by the same time gives the smaller average velocity.

slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which quantity depends on the path and which depends only on where you started and where you ended.

slides.heading: Average and instantaneous values
slides.body_md: **Average velocity** over an interval $= \dfrac{\text{total displacement}}{\text{total time}}$. If the velocity changes, the speed shown at one particular moment is the **instantaneous speed**, and with its direction it is the **instantaneous velocity**. When velocity does not change with time, the body has **uniform velocity**. For a body moving in a straight line without turning back, the size of the average velocity equals the average speed.

rows: Cricket ball at its highest point
Runner round a 400 m track, one lap
average velocity is zero (back at start)
Car on a straight, empty highway at steady speed

visual.alt: Table showing the difference between average and instantaneous values in four situations

slides.narration: Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time. Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one particular moment, like the reading of a speedometer along with the direction. A runner who completes one lap of a track and returns to the start has zero average velocity, because the displacement is zero, even though her speed was never zero.

slides.heading: Acceleration
slides.body_md: **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, where $u$ is the initial velocity, $v$ the final velocity and $t$ the time taken. Its SI unit is metre per second squared ($\text{m s}^{-2}$). Speeding up along the direction of motion gives positive acceleration. Slowing down gives negative acceleration, called **retardation** or deceleration. If the velocity changes by equal amounts in equal times, the acceleration is **uniform**.

rows: Train pulling out of a station
Car moving steadily on a straight road

visual.alt: Table of four motions with the change in velocity and the sign of the acceleration

slides.narration: Acceleration tells us how quickly velocity changes. We find it by subtracting the starting velocity from the final velocity and dividing by the time taken. The unit is metre per second squared. A train pulling out of a station has positive acceleration. A cyclist braking has negative acceleration, which we call retardation. A car at steady velocity has no acceleration at all.

slides.heading: Worked example: acceleration
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An auto-rickshaw speeds up from 18 km/h to 54 km/h in 5.0 s. Then the driver brakes and stops in 3.0 s from 54 km/h. Find both accelerations.

**Step 1: convert to SI.** $18\ \text{km/h} = 18/3.6 = 5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $54\ \text{km/h} = 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Step 2: speeding up.** $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{15 - 5}{5.0} = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Step 3: braking.** $a = \dfrac{0 - 15}{3.0} = -5.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. The minus sign shows retardation.

visual.alt: Table of the two stages of an auto-rickshaw journey with their accelerations of plus 2.0 and minus 5.0 metres per second squared

slides.narration: Always convert to SI units first. Eighteen kilometres per hour is five metres per second, and fifty-four is fifteen. While speeding up, the change in velocity is ten metres per second in five seconds, which gives a positive acceleration of two. While braking, the velocity falls by fifteen in three seconds. The answer is negative, which tells us it is a retardation.

slides.body_md: In a **position–time graph** the time is on the horizontal axis and the position on the vertical axis. A flat line means the body is at rest. A straight sloping line means uniform velocity. A curve that gets steeper means the body is speeding up.

visual.caption: The slope of a position–time graph is the velocity.

slides.narration: A position-time graph puts time along the bottom and position up the side. If the line is flat, the position does not change, so the body is at rest. If the line is straight and sloping, the position changes by equal amounts in equal times, which is uniform velocity. If the line curves and gets steeper, the body covers more distance every second, so it is speeding up.

slides.heading: Slope of a position–time graph is velocity
slides.body_md: The **slope** of a position–time graph is $\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, and that is exactly the velocity. For a straight line the slope is the same everywhere, so the velocity is uniform. A steeper line means a larger speed, and a line sloping downward means the body is moving in the negative direction. For a curve, the slope of the tangent at a point gives the instantaneous velocity.

visual.alt: Position-time graph of a cyclist moving at constant velocity: a straight line from 10 metres at time zero to 50 metres at 8 seconds, slope 5 metres per second
visual.caption: Slope = (50 − 10) m ÷ (8 − 0) s = 5 m/s.

slides.narration: The slope of a position-time graph is the change in position divided by the change in time, and that is the velocity. The line shown rises from ten metres to fifty metres over eight seconds. The slope is therefore forty metres divided by eight seconds, five metres per second. A steeper line would mean a faster body. A line sloping downward would mean motion in the opposite direction.

slides.heading: Worked example: average velocity from a graph
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The position–time graph of a car on a straight road is a straight line passing through (2 s, 30 m) and (10 s, 110 m). Find its average velocity, and its position at $t = 6$ s.

**Step 1.** Average velocity $= \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{110 - 30}{10 - 2} = \dfrac{80}{8} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** The graph is a straight line, so the velocity is uniform. At $t = 6$ s, which is 4 s after the first point, $x = 30 + 10 \times 4 = 70$ m.

visual.alt: Table of readings from the position-time graph of the car and the slope 10 metres per second

slides.narration: To find the average velocity from a graph, pick two clear points on the line. The position changes by eighty metres while the time changes by eight seconds. Dividing gives ten metres per second. Because the line is straight, the velocity is uniform, so we can also find the position at any other time. Four seconds after the first point, the car has moved another forty metres.

slides.heading: Velocity–time graphs
slides.body_md: In a **velocity–time graph**, velocity is on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. A horizontal line means uniform velocity (zero acceleration). A straight line sloping up means uniform positive acceleration, and sloping down means uniform retardation. The **slope** of the line is the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$.

visual.alt: Table of four shapes of velocity-time graphs with what each means for the motion

slides.narration: In a velocity-time graph the height of the line is the velocity. A horizontal line means the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero. A straight rising line means the velocity grows by the same amount every second, which is uniform acceleration. A falling line means uniform retardation. In every case, the slope of the line is the acceleration.

slides.heading: Area under a velocity–time graph is displacement
slides.body_md: The area between the velocity–time line and the time axis is the **displacement**. Split a complicated shape into triangles and rectangles, find each area, and add. For a scooter: triangle $\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 5 = 25$ m, rectangle $10 \times 15 = 150$ m, triangle $\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 10 = 50$ m.

slides.narration: Here is the velocity-time graph of a scooter. In the first five seconds it speeds up to ten metres per second. Then it moves steadily for fifteen seconds. Finally it slows down to rest in ten seconds. The area under the graph is the displacement. Split it into two triangles and one rectangle, find each area, and add them to get the total distance.

slides.heading: Worked example: using the scooter graph
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Use the scooter graph to find the total distance, the average speed over 30 s and the acceleration in the first 5 s and in the last 10 s.

**Step 1: distance** $= 25 + 150 + 50 = 225$ m.

**Step 2: average speed** $= 225 / 30 = 7.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Step 3: first 5 s.** $a = \dfrac{10 - 0}{5} = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Step 4: last 10 s.** $a = \dfrac{0 - 10}{10} = -1.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ (retardation).

visual.alt: Table of the areas under the scooter graph and the resulting average speed of 7.5 metres per second

slides.narration: Reading the graph in parts makes the work easy. The three areas are twenty-five, one hundred and fifty and fifty metres, so the scooter travels two hundred and twenty-five metres. Dividing by the thirty seconds of the journey gives an average speed of seven and a half metres per second. The slopes give the accelerations: two while speeding up and minus one while slowing down.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Distance is the path length (scalar); displacement is the straight-line change of position with direction (vector); both are in metres.
Speed $=$ distance ÷ time; velocity $=$ displacement ÷ time; the SI unit is m s⁻¹ (divide km/h by 3.6).
Acceleration $a = (v - u)/t$ in m s⁻²; it is negative for retardation.
Position–time graph: slope is velocity; flat means at rest.
Velocity–time graph: slope is acceleration; area under the line is displacement.

visual.alt: Table of what the slope and the area of position-time and velocity-time graphs give

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Distance is the path length and displacement is the straight-line change of position with direction. Speed uses distance and velocity uses displacement, both in metres per second. Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. On a position-time graph the slope is the velocity. On a velocity-time graph the slope is the acceleration and the area is the displacement.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Convert km/h to m/s before using any formula (divide by 3.6).
Write the unit in every step, and give a sign or direction for vectors.
On a graph, write down which two points you used for the slope.
For a trapezium or odd shape, split it into rectangles and triangles and show each area.
Average speed is total distance over total time; do not just average the speeds.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Change kilometres per hour to metres per second first. Write the unit in every line of your working. When you read a slope from a graph, say which two points you used. Split odd shapes into rectangles and triangles. And remember that average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the plain average of two speeds.

slides.heading: Equations of motion and circular motion
slides.body_md: Part 2: three equations that link velocity, acceleration, time and displacement, and the special case of motion in a circle.

visual.alt: Table of the three equations of motion with the quantities they link and the one that is missing

slides.narration: In this part we meet the three equations of motion. They work whenever a body moves in a straight line with uniform acceleration, such as a braking truck or a ball thrown up. We derive each one from the velocity-time graph and also by simple algebra. Then we turn to motion in a circle, and find a neat formula for the speed.

slides.heading: Uniform acceleration on a v–t graph
slides.body_md: A body starts with velocity $u$. After time $t$ its velocity is $v$. The graph is a straight line AB. The **slope** is the acceleration $a$, and the **area** under AB is the displacement $s$. The area is a rectangle (height $u$, width $t$) plus a triangle (height $v - u$, width $t$).

visual.caption: The area under the line is the displacement; the slope is the acceleration.

slides.narration: Here is the velocity-time graph of a body with uniform acceleration. It starts at the initial velocity and ends at the final velocity after a time. The straight line has a slope equal to the acceleration. The area under the line is the displacement, and it splits neatly into a rectangle and a triangle. These two ideas give us all three equations.

slides.heading: First equation: v = u + at
slides.body_md:
**Graphical.** Slope of AB $= a = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$. **Algebraic.** By definition, acceleration is the change of velocity per unit time: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$. Rearranging gives
$$v = u + at$$

visual.alt: Flow showing how the slope of the velocity-time graph leads to v equals u plus a t

slides.narration: For the first equation, read the slope of the graph. The slope is the rise in velocity divided by the time, and that is the acceleration. Multiply both sides by the time to get the gain in velocity. Add the starting velocity and we have the first equation: the final velocity equals the initial velocity plus the acceleration times the time.

slides.heading: Second equation: s = ut + ½at²
slides.body_md:
**Graphical.** $s = \text{area of rectangle} + \text{area of triangle} = ut + \tfrac12 (v - u)\,t$. Since $v - u = at$, this becomes
$$s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$$
**Algebraic.** The average velocity is $\dfrac{u + v}{2}$, so $s = \dfrac{u + v}{2}\,t$. Put $v = u + at$ to get the same result.

rows: Area of triangle = ½ (v − u) t
s = u t + ½ a t²
s = u t + ½ a t²

visual.alt: Table comparing the graphical and the algebraic derivation of s equals u t plus half a t squared

slides.narration: For the second equation, use the area under the graph. The rectangle has an area of initial velocity times time. The triangle has an area of half the gain in velocity times time. Replace the gain in velocity by acceleration times time. Adding the two areas gives the second equation. The algebraic method uses the average velocity and the first equation and reaches the same result.

slides.heading: Third equation: v² = u² + 2as
slides.body_md:
The area of the trapezium OABD is $s = \dfrac{u + v}{2} \times t$. From the first equation $t = \dfrac{v - u}{a}$. Substituting,
$$s = \dfrac{(u + v)(v - u)}{2a} = \dfrac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$$
so $2as = v^2 - u^2$, that is
$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

visual.alt: Flow showing how eliminating time gives v squared equals u squared plus 2 a s

slides.narration: The third equation does not contain time. Start with the area of the trapezium, which is the average velocity times the time. Then replace the time using the first equation. Multiply out and the two velocities combine into a difference of squares. Rearranging gives the final velocity squared equals the initial velocity squared plus twice the acceleration times the displacement.

slides.heading: Quick check: choose the equation
slides.body_md: Pick the equation that has the unknown and does not contain a quantity you do not know.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look at what is given and what is asked, and pick the equation that contains exactly those quantities.

slides.heading: Which equation should I use?
slides.body_md: These equations hold only for **uniform acceleration in a straight line**. Write down what is given and what is wanted, then choose the equation that does not contain the quantity you neither know nor need. Take the direction of $u$ as positive; retardation then has a negative $a$.

visual.alt: Table showing which equation of motion to use for different known and unknown quantities

slides.narration: Choosing the right equation saves time. First write down what is given and what is asked. If time is missing, use the third equation. If the final velocity is missing, use the second. If the displacement is not needed, use the first. Remember that these equations are only for uniform acceleration along a straight line, and take the starting direction as positive.

slides.heading: Worked example: braking distance
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A car moving at $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is braked with a uniform retardation of $3.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find the time taken to stop and the braking distance.

**Given.** $u = 15$, $v = 0$, $a = -3.0$ (SI units).

**Step 1: time.** $v = u + at \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{0 - 15}{-3.0} = 5.0$ s.

**Step 2: distance (no time needed).** $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \Rightarrow 0 = 225 + 2(-3.0)s \Rightarrow s = 37.5$ m.

**Check.** $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2 = 15(5.0) - \tfrac12 (3.0)(25) = 75 - 37.5 = 37.5$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the given and found quantities for a car braking from 15 metres per second: time 5.0 seconds and distance 37.5 metres

slides.narration: Write down what we know. The initial velocity is fifteen, the final velocity is zero and the acceleration is minus three. The first equation gives the time to stop, five seconds. The third equation gives the braking distance directly without using time, thirty-seven point five metres. We can confirm it with the second equation, which gives the same answer.

slides.heading: Worked example: a ball thrown upward
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A ball is thrown straight up at $19.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downward and ignore air resistance. Find the time to reach the top, the greatest height and the total time in the air.

**Take up as positive:** $u = 19.6$, $a = -9.8$, and $v = 0$ at the top.

**Time to top.** $t = \dfrac{0 - 19.6}{-9.8} = 2.0$ s.

**Greatest height.** $s = \dfrac{0 - 19.6^2}{2(-9.8)} = 19.6$ m.

**Total time** $= 2 \times 2.0 = 4.0$ s, and it returns with speed $19.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Velocity-time graph of a ball thrown straight up at 19.6 metres per second: a straight line sloping down at 9.8 metres per second every second, crossing zero at 2 seconds and reaching minus 19.6 at 4 seconds
visual.caption: Slope = −9.8 m/s² (g); the line crosses zero at the top of the flight.

slides.narration: When a ball goes up, gravity slows it down by nine point eight metres per second every second. Taking up as positive, the acceleration is minus nine point eight. The ball stops at the top after two seconds, having risen nineteen point six metres. The fall takes another two seconds, so the total time in the air is four seconds. It returns to the hand with the same speed it left with.

slides.heading: Quick check: a ball thrown up
slides.body_md: Think about the velocity and the acceleration at the top of the flight.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think carefully about what happens to the velocity and the acceleration at the very top of the flight.

slides.heading: Worked example: a train gaining speed
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A train moving at $5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ gains speed uniformly at $0.2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ for 50 s. Find its final speed and the distance covered.

**Step 1.** $v = u + at = 5 + 0.2 \times 50 = 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2 = 5 \times 50 + \tfrac12 \times 0.2 \times 50^2 = 250 + 250 = 500$ m.

**Check with the average velocity.** $\dfrac{5 + 15}{2} \times 50 = 10 \times 50 = 500$ m.

visual.alt: Table showing three ways of finding that the train covers 500 metres

slides.narration: The train starts at five metres per second and gains point two metres per second every second for fifty seconds. The first equation gives a final speed of fifteen. The second equation gives the distance as two hundred and fifty plus another two hundred and fifty, five hundred metres. A good habit is to check with the average velocity, ten metres per second, times fifty seconds.

slides.heading: Uniform circular motion
slides.body_md: When a body moves in a circle at **constant speed**, the motion is called **uniform circular motion**. The speed is constant, but the **direction of the velocity changes at every point**: it is always along the **tangent** to the circle. Examples: a satellite in orbit, the tip of a fan blade, a stone whirled on a string, a merry-go-round.

slides.narration: Now we turn to circular motion. When a body moves round a circle at constant speed, the motion is called uniform circular motion. The speed does not change, but the velocity does, because its direction keeps changing. At every point the velocity points along the tangent to the circle, at right angles to the radius. A satellite and the tip of a fan blade are both good examples.

slides.heading: Deriving v = 2πr / T
slides.body_md:
The **period** $T$ is the time for one complete revolution. In one revolution the body covers the circumference $2\pi r$. Since speed is distance divided by time,
$$v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$$
The speed is in m s⁻¹ if $r$ is in metres and $T$ in seconds. If the body makes $f$ revolutions every second, $T = 1/f$ and $v = 2\pi r f$.

visual.alt: Flow from the circumference and the period to the speed v equals 2 pi r over T

slides.narration: To find the speed in a circle, use the basic idea that speed is distance divided by time. In one full round the body covers the circumference of the circle, two pi times the radius. The time for one round is called the period. Dividing the circumference by the period gives the speed. A larger circle or a shorter period means a greater speed.

slides.heading: Worked example: the Moon in orbit
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The Moon goes round the Earth in a nearly circular orbit of radius about $3.84 \times 10^{8}$ m, taking about 27.3 days for one revolution. Find its orbital speed.

**Step 1: period in seconds.** $T = 27.3 \times 24 \times 3600 = 2.36 \times 10^{6}$ s.

**Step 2.** $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14 \times 3.84 \times 10^{8}}{2.36 \times 10^{6}} \approx 1020\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, about 1.0 km s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the Moon orbit: radius, period, circumference and the speed of about 1000 metres per second

slides.narration: Let us find how fast the Moon moves. Its orbit has a radius of about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres and one revolution takes about twenty-seven days. First change the period into seconds. Then divide the circumference of the orbit by the period. The Moon moves at about one thousand metres per second, which is about one kilometre every second.

slides.heading: Circular motion is accelerated motion
slides.body_md: Even at constant speed, a body in a circle has **changing velocity**, because the direction changes. Changing velocity means **acceleration**. This acceleration points towards the centre of the circle, so we say that uniform circular motion is **accelerated motion**.

rows: the ride turns at a steady rate
orbit is almost a perfect circle
fan runs at a steady speed

visual.alt: Table of four examples of uniform circular motion

slides.narration: Here is a point that surprises many students. A body in uniform circular motion has constant speed, yet it is accelerating. Acceleration means a change in velocity, and velocity includes direction. In a circle the direction changes at every moment, so the velocity changes. This acceleration is directed towards the centre of the circle.

slides.body_md: Apply v = 2πr/T to a body moving in a circle.

bullets: For uniform acceleration in a straight line: $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
Derived from the v–t graph: slope is a, area is s (rectangle plus triangle).
Take the starting direction as positive; retardation gives negative a.
Free fall: $a = g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downward; a ball thrown up stops at the top and returns with the same speed.
Uniform circular motion: constant speed $v = 2\pi r / T$, but the velocity changes direction, so it is accelerated motion.

visual.alt: Table of the values of u, v and a in three common situations

slides.narration: To sum up. For uniform acceleration in a straight line we have three equations, derived from the area and the slope of the velocity-time graph. The direction of the starting velocity is taken as positive. Free fall has an acceleration of nine point eight metres per second squared downward. In a circle, the speed is the circumference divided by the period, and the velocity keeps changing direction.

sections.heading: 1. Distance and displacement
sections.body_md:
A body is in motion if its position changes with time, measured against a chosen reference point. The SI unit of length is the metre (m).

- **Distance** is the total length of the path. It is a scalar: size only, never negative.
- **Displacement** is the shortest straight-line change of position from start to end, with its direction. It is a vector.
- Displacement can be smaller than the distance (a curved or bent path), equal to it (straight line, no turning back), or zero (the body returns to its start).

Shortest change of position from start to end, with direction; a vector quantity.
A quantity with both size and direction.

sections.heading: 2. Speed, velocity and acceleration
sections.body_md:
**Speed** $=$ distance ÷ time (scalar). **Velocity** $=$ displacement ÷ time (vector). Both are in m s⁻¹. To change km/h to m/s divide by 3.6.

**Average velocity** is total displacement over total time; **instantaneous velocity** is the velocity at a particular moment. Velocity is **uniform** if neither size nor direction changes.

**Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity, $a = (v - u)/t$, in m s⁻². Speeding up gives positive acceleration, slowing down negative acceleration (**retardation**). A body can have zero velocity at an instant and still be accelerating, as a ball does at the top of its flight.

key_terms.definition_md: Total displacement divided by total time taken.
Velocity at one particular instant of time.
Change in velocity per unit time; SI unit m s⁻².
Negative acceleration: the body is slowing down.

sections.heading: 3. Position–time graphs
sections.body_md:
Time goes on the x-axis and position on the y-axis.

- A flat line: the body is at rest.
- A straight sloping line: uniform velocity. **Slope $= \Delta x / \Delta t =$ velocity.**
- A line sloping down: motion in the negative direction.
- A curve that steepens: increasing velocity (the body is accelerating).

To find the **average velocity** from a graph, choose two points on it and divide the change in position by the change in time.

Rise divided by run; on a position–time graph it equals velocity.

sections.heading: 4. Velocity–time graphs
sections.body_md:
Time goes on the x-axis and velocity on the y-axis.

- A horizontal line: uniform velocity, zero acceleration.
- A straight rising line: uniform acceleration; a straight falling line: uniform retardation.
- **Slope $=$ acceleration.**
- **Area between the line and the time axis $=$ displacement.** Split an irregular shape into rectangles and triangles. If part of the graph lies below the axis, that area is a displacement in the opposite direction.

For a scooter that speeds up to 10 m s⁻¹ in 5 s, runs steadily for 15 s and stops in 10 s, the total area is $25 + 150 + 50 = 225$ m.

sections.heading: 5. Equations of motion for uniform acceleration
sections.body_md:
For motion in a straight line with constant acceleration $a$, initial velocity $u$, final velocity $v$, time $t$ and displacement $s$:

$$v = u + at \qquad s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2 \qquad v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

**Graphical derivation.** On the $v$–$t$ line AB, slope $= (v - u)/t = a$ gives the first. The area under AB is a rectangle $ut$ plus a triangle $\tfrac12 (v - u)t$, and $v - u = at$ gives the second. Eliminating $t$ between $s = \tfrac12 (u + v)t$ and $t = (v - u)/a$ gives the third.

**Algebraic derivation.** The definition $a = (v - u)/t$ gives the first. With average velocity $(u + v)/2$, $s = \tfrac12 (u + v) t$, and putting in $v = u + at$ gives the second.

Take the direction of $u$ as positive. Applications: braking distance of a vehicle, a train gaining speed.

sections.heading: 6. Free fall and uniform circular motion
sections.body_md:
**Free fall.** Near the Earth's surface a falling body gains about $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ of velocity every second (acceleration due to gravity $g$), whatever its mass, when air resistance is small. A ball thrown up with $u$ rises until $v = 0$ at height $u^2 / 2g$ after $u/g$ seconds and returns with the same speed.

**Uniform circular motion.** A body moving in a circle of radius $r$ at constant speed covers the circumference $2\pi r$ in one period $T$:
$$v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$$
The speed is constant but the direction of the velocity (along the tangent) changes continually, so the motion is **accelerated**, with the acceleration directed towards the centre. Examples: a satellite, a merry-go-round, the tip of a fan blade.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Convert km/h to m/s (divide by 3.6) before using any formula.
- Write what is given with its sign (u, v, a, t, s), then choose the equation.
- On a graph, say which two points you used for the slope and show each area you add.
- Remember: a ball at the top of its flight has zero velocity but acceleration 9.8 m s⁻² downward.
- Circular motion: speed is constant, velocity is not, so it is accelerated.

cards.front_md: Distance versus displacement?
cards.back_md: Distance is the path length (scalar). Displacement is the straight-line change of position with direction (vector).

cards.front_md: SI unit of displacement?
cards.back_md: Metre (m).

cards.front_md: Can displacement be zero when distance is not?
cards.back_md: Yes. A runner who completes a lap returns to the start: displacement zero, distance equal to the lap length.

cards.front_md: Speed versus velocity?
cards.back_md: Speed is distance ÷ time (scalar). Velocity is displacement ÷ time (vector).

cards.front_md: SI unit of speed and velocity?
cards.back_md: Metre per second, $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: How do you change km/h to m/s?
cards.back_md: Divide by 3.6. For example $72\ \text{km/h} = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: What is average velocity?
cards.back_md: Total displacement divided by total time.

cards.front_md: What is instantaneous velocity?
cards.back_md: The velocity of a body at one particular instant, such as a speedometer reading with direction.

cards.front_md: Define acceleration.
cards.back_md: The rate of change of velocity: $a = (v - u)/t$. SI unit $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

cards.front_md: What is retardation?
cards.back_md: Negative acceleration: the body slows down.

cards.front_md: What does uniform acceleration mean?
cards.back_md: Velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.

cards.front_md: What does a flat line on a position–time graph mean?
cards.back_md: The body is at rest.

cards.front_md: What does the slope of a position–time graph give?
cards.back_md: The velocity.

cards.front_md: What does a straight sloping line on a position–time graph show?
cards.back_md: Uniform velocity.

cards.front_md: What does the slope of a velocity–time graph give?
cards.back_md: The acceleration.

cards.front_md: What does the area under a velocity–time graph give?
cards.back_md: The displacement.

cards.front_md: What does a horizontal line on a v–t graph show?
cards.back_md: Uniform velocity, zero acceleration.

cards.front_md: How do you find average velocity from a position–time graph?
cards.back_md: Divide the change in position by the change in time between two points: $(x_2 - x_1)/(t_2 - t_1)$.

cards.front_md: First equation of motion?
cards.back_md: $v = u + at$

cards.front_md: Second equation of motion?
cards.back_md: $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$

cards.front_md: Third equation of motion?
When do the equations of motion hold?
cards.back_md: For motion in a straight line with uniform acceleration.

cards.front_md: Which equation has no time in it?
How is s = ut + ½at² found from the v–t graph?
cards.back_md: Area = rectangle (u t) + triangle (½ (v − u) t), and v − u = a t.

cards.front_md: Value of g used in Class 9?
cards.back_md: $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, directed downward.

cards.front_md: Velocity and acceleration of a ball at the top of its flight?
cards.back_md: Velocity is zero; acceleration is still $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downward.

cards.front_md: Height reached by a ball thrown up at speed u?
cards.back_md: $H = u^2/2g$, reached after $t = u/g$.

cards.front_md: What is uniform circular motion?
cards.back_md: Motion in a circle at constant speed.

cards.front_md: Speed of a body in uniform circular motion?
cards.back_md: $v = 2\pi r / T$

cards.front_md: Is uniform circular motion accelerated?
cards.back_md: Yes. The speed is constant but the direction of velocity changes, so the velocity changes.

cards.front_md: Direction of the velocity in circular motion?
cards.back_md: Along the tangent to the circle, at right angles to the radius.

cards.front_md: Exam tip for acceleration problems?
cards.back_md: Convert to SI units, take the starting direction as positive, and give the sign of a.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist rides once round a circular park of circumference 400 m and stops at the gate where she began. Which of these quantities is zero?
questions.solution_md: She ends where she started, so the straight-line change of position, the displacement, is zero — option (d). The distance is 400 m, so her average speed is not zero, and the ride took some time.

questions.stem_md: The speedometer of a motorbike on a highway near Nagpur reads 36 km/h. In SI units this speed is:
questions.solution_md: $36\ \text{km/h} = 36 \times \dfrac{1000}{3600} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ — option (c). Option (b) multiplies by 3.6 instead of dividing, and (d) divides by 60.

questions.stem_md: A boy walks along a semicircular track of diameter 140 m from one end A to the other end B. Take $\pi = 22/7$. The distance he covers and the magnitude of his displacement are:
questions.solution_md: The path is half a circle of radius 70 m: distance $= \pi r = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 70 = 220$ m. The displacement is the straight line AB, equal to the diameter, 140 m — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which one of these quantities needs a direction, as well as a size, to be described completely?
questions.solution_md: Velocity is displacement per unit time and is a vector, so a direction is needed — option (a). Speed, distance and time are scalars.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist moving towards the east on a straight lane applies the brakes steadily and comes to a stop. The direction of her acceleration is:

options.text_md: there is no direction because it is zero

questions.solution_md: Her velocity decreases while she moves east, so the change of velocity points west and the acceleration is opposite to the motion, a retardation — option (b). It is not zero because the velocity is changing.

questions.stem_md: The velocity of a body changes uniformly from $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $16\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 3 s along a straight line. The distance it covers in these 3 s is:
questions.solution_md: For uniform acceleration the average velocity is $(4 + 16)/2 = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so the distance is $10 \times 3 = 30$ m — option (b). (a) uses only the starting velocity and (c) only the final velocity.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A body that moves with a constant speed cannot have a changing velocity.
questions.solution_md: False. Velocity includes direction. A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a velocity that changes direction all the time.

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of acceleration is ___.
questions.solution_md: Acceleration is change of velocity (m s⁻¹) per unit time (s), so its unit is **metre per second squared** (m s⁻²).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A runner who completes exactly one lap of a 400 m track has an average velocity of zero.

**Reason (R):** Average velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken, and the displacement for a full lap is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Back at the starting point, the displacement is zero, so average velocity $=$ displacement ÷ time is zero although the distance is 400 m. R is the reason for A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A satellite orbiting the Earth at constant speed has no acceleration.

**Reason (R):** The direction of the satellite’s velocity changes continuously as it moves along the orbit.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the changing direction of the velocity means the velocity changes, so the satellite is accelerating. R is true and is exactly why A is false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A bus travels 60 km in the first 1.5 h of a trip and then 40 km in the next 0.5 h on the same road. Find its average speed for the whole trip, in m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Total distance $= 60 + 40 = 100$ km; total time $= 1.5 + 0.5 = 2$ h. Average speed $= 100 / 2 = 50$ km/h $= 50 / 3.6 = 13.9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

marking_scheme.step: Total distance over total time = 50 km/h

questions.stem_md: A jogger starts at corner A of a rectangular park 80 m long and 60 m wide and runs along the two sides to the opposite corner C in 50 s. Find the magnitude of her average velocity, in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Displacement = the diagonal $AC = \sqrt{80^2 + 60^2} = 100$ m (the path length is 140 m). Average velocity $= 100 / 50 = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: An electric train leaving Surat station speeds up from rest to 72 km/h in 40 s along a straight track. Find its average acceleration, in m s⁻².
A taxi completes one full round of a circular roundabout of circumference 200 m in 20 s. Find its average speed and its average velocity for this round trip, and say why they are different.

answer.model_answer_md: The average speed is distance ÷ time $= 200/20 = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. After a full round the taxi is back at its starting point, so the displacement is zero and the average velocity is zero. They differ because speed uses the path length, whereas velocity uses the displacement.

questions.solution_md: Distance 200 m gives 10 m/s; displacement zero gives zero average velocity.

marking_scheme.step: Average speed 10 m s⁻¹ and average velocity 0

questions.stem_md: The velocity of a car falls uniformly from 20 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s. Calculate its acceleration and say what the sign of your answer shows.

answer.model_answer_md: $a = (v - u)/t = (10 - 20)/5.0 = -2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. The negative sign shows that the acceleration is opposite to the direction of motion, so the car is slowing down: it has a retardation of $2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

questions.solution_md: Substitute in a = (v − u)/t; negative means retardation.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist rounds a bend in the road at a steady speed of 5 m s⁻¹. Is she accelerating? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Yes. Although her speed is steady, the direction of her motion changes as she goes round the bend. Velocity has both size and direction, so her velocity changes, and a changing velocity means she has an acceleration.

questions.solution_md: Acceleration is change of velocity, and velocity includes direction.

marking_scheme.step: A change in velocity means acceleration

questions.stem_md: A car’s odometer reads 12 560 km at the start and 12 640 km at the end of a 2.0 h trip between two cities. The straight-line distance between the cities is 60 km. Find the average speed and the magnitude of the average velocity in km/h, and explain why they differ.

answer.model_answer_md: The distance is $12\,640 - 12\,560 = 80$ km, so the average speed is $80/2.0 = 40$ km/h. The displacement is the straight-line distance of 60 km, so the magnitude of the average velocity is $60/2.0 = 30$ km/h. The values differ because the road is not straight: the path length is greater than the size of the displacement, so speed is greater than the size of the velocity.

questions.solution_md: Distance 80 km gives 40 km/h; displacement 60 km gives 30 km/h; the path is longer than the straight line.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: path length is greater than displacement

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define distance and displacement, stating which is a scalar and which a vector.

(b) A tourist walks 300 m east along a lane and then 400 m north to a temple in 10 minutes. Find the distance, the displacement and the average speed in m s⁻¹.

(c) State one situation in which the distance and the magnitude of the displacement are equal.

answer.model_answer_md: Distance is the length of the path travelled, a scalar. Displacement is the shortest straight-line change of position from start to end with direction, a vector. In (b) the distance is $300 + 400 = 700$ m. The displacement is $\sqrt{300^2 + 400^2} = 500$ m, about $53^\circ$ north of east. The time is $10 \times 60 = 600$ s, so the average speed is $700/600 = 1.17\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. In (c), distance equals the magnitude of displacement for motion along a straight line in one direction, such as a car moving straight along an empty road.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; 700 m, 500 m, 1.17 m/s; straight-line motion in one direction.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Both definitions with scalar and vector

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
Meera records the position of a cyclist moving on a straight canal road from a marker post. Positions are measured eastward from the post.

| Time t (s) | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position x (m) | 0 | 50 | 50 | 50 | 10 |

The graph of position against time is made of straight-line pieces joining these points.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) 10 s to 30 s

**(b)** The velocity is 5.0 m s⁻¹ towards the east.

**(c)** (i) The displacement is $10 - 0 = 10$ m eastward, so the average velocity $= 10/40 = 0.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ eastward.

**OR** (ii) She goes 50 m east, rests, then comes back 40 m, so the distance is $50 + 40 = 90$ m and the average speed is $90/40 = 2.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Between 10 s and 30 s the position stays at 50 m, so the graph is flat and the velocity is zero — option (a).

**(b)** $v = (50 - 0)/(10 - 0) = 5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ eastward.

**(c)** (i) Displacement divided by total time.

(ii) Add the lengths of the pieces of the path; divide by 40 s.

children.stem_md: During which interval is the cyclist at rest?

options.text_md: The cyclist is never at rest

children.solution_md: Between 10 s and 30 s the position stays at 50 m, so the graph is flat and the velocity is zero — option (a).

children.stem_md: Find the velocity of the cyclist during the first 10 s.

answer.model_answer_md: The velocity is 5.0 m s⁻¹ towards the east.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Find the average velocity of the cyclist over the whole 40 s.

answer.model_answer_md: The displacement is $10 - 0 = 10$ m eastward, so the average velocity $= 10/40 = 0.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ eastward.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Find the distance covered by the cyclist in the 40 s and her average speed.

answer.model_answer_md: She goes 50 m east, rests, then comes back 40 m, so the distance is $50 + 40 = 90$ m and the average speed is $90/40 = 2.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

alternatives.solution_md: Add the lengths of the pieces of the path; divide by 40 s.

questions.stem_md: The position–time graph of a toy car is a straight line that slopes upward. The car is moving with:
questions.solution_md: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so the velocity is constant, that is uniform velocity — option (c). A flat line would mean zero velocity and a steepening curve increasing velocity.

questions.stem_md: The velocity–time graph of a trolley is a horizontal line at $6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 8$ s. The displacement of the trolley in this time is:
questions.solution_md: The area of the rectangle under the line is $6 \times 8 = 48$ m — option (a). (d) wrongly divides 8 by 6.

questions.stem_md: On the same position–time axes, the line for car A is steeper than the line for car B, and both slope upward. This shows that:

options.text_md: car B has a greater velocity than car A
car A and car B have the same velocity
car A has a greater velocity than car B
car A has acceleration but car B has none

questions.solution_md: The slope of a position–time graph is the velocity, so the steeper line means a greater velocity — option (c). Two straight lines both mean uniform velocity, so neither car is accelerating.

questions.stem_md: The velocity–time graph of a train is a straight line that slopes downward but stays above the time axis. During this time the train is:
questions.solution_md: The line is above the axis, so the velocity is positive (forward). The line slopes down, so the velocity decreases: a uniform retardation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The slope of a position–time graph gives the acceleration of the body.
questions.solution_md: False. The slope of a position–time graph is the velocity. The slope of a velocity–time graph is the acceleration.

questions.stem_md: The area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis gives the ___ of the body.
questions.solution_md: The area under a velocity–time graph is the **displacement** (it is the distance when the body does not turn back).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The slope of a straight line on a velocity–time graph gives the acceleration.

**Reason (R):** Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: The slope is rise ÷ run $= \Delta v / \Delta t$, which is the definition of acceleration, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each line on a velocity–time graph (Column A) with the motion it shows (Column B).

options.text_md: A horizontal line above the time axis
A straight line falling towards the time axis
A line lying along the time axis

questions.solution_md: A horizontal line means constant velocity, a rising line means growing velocity, a falling line means slowing down, and a line on the axis means zero velocity.

questions.stem_md: The position–time graph of a tractor is a straight line passing through the points (3 s, 18 m) and (11 s, 66 m). Find the velocity of the tractor, in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Velocity = slope $= \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \dfrac{66 - 18}{11 - 3} = \dfrac{48}{8} = 6.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

marking_scheme.step: Reads the two points and finds Δx = 48 m and Δt = 8 s

questions.stem_md: The velocity–time graph of a tractor in a field in Punjab is a trapezium. Its velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 4.0 m s⁻¹ in 5 s, stays constant for 20 s and then falls uniformly to zero in 5 s. Find the total distance it covers, in m.
questions.solution_md: Distance = total area under the graph. First triangle $= \tfrac12 \times 4 \times 5 = 10$ m; rectangle $= 4 \times 20 = 80$ m; last triangle $= \tfrac12 \times 4 \times 5 = 10$ m. Total $= 10 + 80 + 10 = 100$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Splits the graph into two triangles and a rectangle

questions.stem_md: A bullock cart moves at a steady 3 m s⁻¹ for 20 s along a straight road. Draw in words the shape of its velocity–time graph, and use the graph to find the distance covered.

answer.model_answer_md: The graph is a horizontal straight line at $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 20$ s. The area of the rectangle under it is the displacement: $3 \times 20 = 60$ m. The slope is zero, which shows there is no acceleration.

questions.solution_md: Horizontal line; area of rectangle 3 × 20 = 60 m.

questions.stem_md: The position–time graph of a bus is a straight line sloping downward. What does this tell you about the motion of the bus? Is the bus accelerating?

answer.model_answer_md: A straight line means the velocity is constant, so the bus has uniform velocity and is not accelerating. A downward slope means the position is decreasing with time, so the bus is moving in the negative direction, back towards the reference point.

questions.solution_md: Straight line: uniform velocity; negative slope: moving in the negative direction.

marking_scheme.step: Negative slope: moving in the negative direction

questions.stem_md:
The velocity–time graph of a cyclist is a trapezium: the velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 4.0 s, stays constant for 10 s and then falls uniformly to zero in 6.0 s.

(a) Find the acceleration in the first 4.0 s and the retardation in the last 6.0 s.

(b) Find the total distance covered and the average speed.

answer.model_answer_md: The acceleration is the slope of the velocity–time graph. In the first part, $a = (8.0 - 0)/4.0 = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. In the last part, $a = (0 - 8.0)/6.0 = -1.33\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, so the retardation is $1.33\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. The distance covered is the area under the graph, which is a trapezium, found by splitting it into parts: first triangle $\tfrac12 \times 8.0 \times 4.0 = 16$ m, rectangle $8.0 \times 10 = 80$ m and last triangle $\tfrac12 \times 8.0 \times 6.0 = 24$ m. The total is $120$ m. The total time is $4.0 + 10 + 6.0 = 20$ s, so the average speed is $120/20 = 6.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

marking_scheme.step: Acceleration 2.0 m s⁻² from the slope

questions.stem_md: Explain how you would find (a) the velocity from a position–time graph and (b) the acceleration and the displacement from a velocity–time graph. Use one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Pick two points on the straight line, then divide the change in position by the change in time. For (0 s, 10 m) and (5 s, 35 m) the velocity is $25/5 = 5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (b) The slope of the velocity–time line is the acceleration: from $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 3 s gives $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. The area under the line is the displacement: $\tfrac12 (2 + 8) \times 3 = 15$ m.

questions.solution_md: Slope of x–t is velocity; slope of v–t is acceleration; area under v–t is displacement.

marking_scheme.step: Velocity from the slope of the x–t graph, with an example
Acceleration from the slope of the v–t graph, with an example
Displacement from the area, with an example

questions.stem_md: A cyclist’s initial speed u, final speed v and acceleration a are known, and the distance s covered is wanted. Time is not given. The equation to use is:
questions.solution_md: The equations in (a), (b) and (d) all contain the unknown time $t$. Only $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ links $u$, $v$, $a$ and $s$ without $t$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: At the highest point of its flight a ball thrown straight up has:

options.text_md: zero velocity and an acceleration of $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downward
an acceleration of $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ upward and zero velocity
a velocity of $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and no acceleration

questions.solution_md: At the top the ball turns round, so its velocity is momentarily zero. Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is 9.8 m s⁻² downward — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which equation of motion is obtained by finding the area under the velocity–time graph of a body in uniform acceleration?
questions.solution_md: The area is a rectangle $ut$ plus a triangle $\tfrac12 at^2$, giving $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$ — option (c). The first equation comes from the slope.

questions.stem_md: Two iron balls, one of mass 1 kg and one of mass 5 kg, are dropped together from a roof. Ignoring air resistance, the ratio of their accelerations as they fall is:
questions.solution_md: In free fall every body has the same acceleration $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, whatever its mass, so the ratio is 1 : 1 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A ball is thrown straight up at $4.9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and caught at the level of release. Taking $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, the time for which it is in the air is:
questions.solution_md: Time to the top $= u/g = 4.9/9.8 = 0.5$ s. The fall takes the same time, so the total is $2 \times 0.5 = 1.0$ s — option (d). (a) is only the upward part.

questions.stem_md: A truck is braked with the same retardation, first from a speed v and then from a speed 3v. Neglecting the driver’s reaction time, the braking distance for the second case is:

options.text_md: three times that for the first case
six times that for the first case
one third of that for the first case
nine times that for the first case

questions.solution_md: With $v_\text{final} = 0$, $s = u^2/(2a)$. Tripling $u$ multiplies $s$ by $3^2 = 9$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The three equations of motion can be used for a ball thrown straight up if the acceleration is taken as −9.8 m s⁻² and upward is positive.
questions.solution_md: True. Gravity gives a uniform acceleration of 9.8 m s⁻² downward, which is −9.8 m s⁻² when up is positive, so the equations hold all the way up and down.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The equation v = u + at holds for a body moving along a straight line with uniform acceleration.

**Reason (R):** The SI unit of acceleration is metre per second squared.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the equation comes from the definition of uniform acceleration. R is also true but it only states the unit, which does not explain why the equation holds — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The distance travelled by a body between two instants can be greater than the magnitude of its displacement.

**Reason (R):** Displacement is always greater than the distance travelled.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: on a bent or curved path the path length exceeds the straight-line displacement. R is false, because the displacement is never greater than the distance — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student has to solve four problems. Match each problem (Column A) with the best equation of motion (Column B).

options.text_md: A truck brakes to rest from a known speed with a known retardation; find the braking distance
Find the speed a car gains in 6 s of uniform acceleration
Find the distance a train covers in 40 s with known u and a
A satellite’s orbit radius and period are known; find its speed

questions.solution_md: Braking distance without time uses v² = u² + 2as; the speed gained uses v = u + at; distance in a given time uses s = ut + ½at²; a speed in a circle uses v = 2πr/T.

questions.stem_md: A truck moving at 90 km/h on a highway near Nagpur is braked with a uniform retardation of 2.5 m s⁻². Find the distance it travels before stopping, in m.
A boy throws a ball vertically upward at 29.4 m s⁻¹. Taking $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ and ignoring air resistance, find the greatest height the ball reaches above his hand, in m.

marking_scheme.step: Takes v = 0 and a = −9.8 m s⁻² at the top

questions.stem_md: A train moving at 10 m s⁻¹ gains speed uniformly and covers 450 m in the next 30 s. Find its acceleration, in m s⁻² (2 significant figures).
Draw the velocity–time graph of a body that moves with uniform acceleration a from initial velocity u to final velocity v in time t, and use it to derive v = u + at.

answer.model_answer_md: Plot velocity on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. The graph is a straight line AB rising from $u$ at $t = 0$ to $v$ at time $t$. The slope of AB is the acceleration, so $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$. Multiplying by $t$ gives $at = v - u$, and therefore $v = u + at$.

questions.solution_md: Draw the line AB; slope = a; rearrange.

marking_scheme.step: Straight-line v–t graph from u to v, labelled

questions.stem_md: Using the area under the velocity–time graph of a body in uniform acceleration, derive the equation s = ut + ½at².

answer.model_answer_md: The displacement $s$ is the area under the line AB. This area is a rectangle of height $u$ and width $t$ plus a triangle of height $v - u$ and base $t$. So $s = ut + \tfrac12 (v - u)t$. Since $v - u = at$ from the first equation, the area of the triangle becomes $\tfrac12 at^2$. Adding the two areas gives $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$.

questions.solution_md: Rectangle ut + triangle ½(v − u)t, with v − u = at.

marking_scheme.step: Area split into a rectangle and a triangle
Replaces v − u by at to get the result

questions.stem_md: Derive the equation v² = u² + 2as for a body in uniform acceleration, starting from the idea that the displacement equals the average velocity multiplied by the time.

answer.model_answer_md: For uniform acceleration the average velocity is $\dfrac{u + v}{2}$, so the displacement is the average velocity multiplied by the time, $s = \dfrac{u + v}{2}\,t$. From the first equation $v = u + at$, the time is $t = \dfrac{v - u}{a}$. Substituting this time into the expression for $s$ gives $s = \dfrac{(u + v)(v - u)}{2a} = \dfrac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}$. Multiplying by $2a$ and rearranging, we get $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

questions.solution_md: Eliminate t between s = (u + v)t/2 and t = (v − u)/a.

marking_scheme.step: (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u² and rearranged

questions.stem_md:
A body moves in a straight line with uniform acceleration a. Its velocity changes from u to v in time t and its displacement is s.

(a) Use the velocity–time graph to derive v = u + at and s = ut + ½at².

(b) Derive v² = u² + 2as by algebra.

answer.model_answer_md: On the velocity–time graph the straight line AB runs from $u$ to $v$ in time $t$. Its slope is the acceleration: $a = (v - u)/t$, so $v = u + at$. The area under AB is the displacement. It is a rectangle $ut$ plus a triangle $\tfrac12 (v - u)t$, and with $v - u = at$ we get $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$. For (b), the average velocity is $(u + v)/2$, so $s = \dfrac{(u + v)}{2}\,t$. Putting in the time $t = (v - u)/a$ from the first equation gives $2as = (u + v)(v - u) = v^2 - u^2$. Hence $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, an equation that does not contain time.

questions.solution_md: Slope gives the first, area gives the second, elimination of t gives the third.

marking_scheme.step: Labelled graph with u, v and t

questions.stem_md:
A stone is dropped from rest from a cliff and strikes the sea after 4.0 s. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and ignore air resistance.

(a) Find the height of the cliff.

(b) Find the speed of the stone just before it hits the water.

(c) Find the distance the stone falls during the last second.

answer.model_answer_md: The stone starts from rest, so its initial velocity is zero and its acceleration is $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downward. (a) The height of the cliff is the distance fallen in 4.0 s: $s = \tfrac12 gt^2 = \tfrac12 (9.8)(16) = 78.4$ m. (b) The speed on reaching the water is $v = gt = 9.8 \times 4.0 = 39.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (c) In the first 3.0 s the stone falls $\tfrac12 (9.8)(9) = 44.1$ m, so the distance fallen in the last second is the difference, $78.4 - 44.1 = 34.3$ m. Notice that this is much more than the 4.9 m fallen in the first second, because the stone keeps speeding up as it falls.

questions.solution_md: Height 78.4 m; speed 39.2 m/s; last second 34.3 m.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Speed 39.2 m s⁻¹ using v = gt
(c) Distance in the last second 34.3 m

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student drops a stone into a dry well and measures the depth fallen with a rangefinder at three instants. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ and ignore air resistance.

| Time after release t (s) | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Depth fallen (m) | 4.9 | 19.6 | 44.1 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) starts from rest and has a constant acceleration, so s is proportional to t²

**(b)** $v = gt = 9.8 \times 3.0 = 29.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**(c)** (i) $s = \tfrac12 gt^2 = \tfrac12 \times 9.8 \times (2.5)^2 = \tfrac12 \times 9.8 \times 6.25 = 30.6$ m (30.625 m).

**OR** (ii) $v^2 = 0 + 2(9.8)(44.1) = 864.4$, so $v = 29.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, the same value as from $v = gt$.

**(b)** From rest $v = u + gt = 0 + 9.8 \times 3.0 = 29.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

children.stem_md: The depths fallen after 1.0 s, 2.0 s and 3.0 s are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9. This is because the stone:

options.text_md: moves at a constant speed, so s is proportional to t
starts from rest and has a constant acceleration, so s is proportional to t²
has an acceleration that doubles every second
starts with a velocity of 9.8 m s⁻¹

children.stem_md: Find the speed of the stone 3.0 s after release, in m s⁻¹.
**Either** (i): A second stone dropped into the well hits the bottom 2.5 s after release. Find the depth of the well.

answer.model_answer_md: $s = \tfrac12 gt^2 = \tfrac12 \times 9.8 \times (2.5)^2 = \tfrac12 \times 9.8 \times 6.25 = 30.6$ m (30.625 m).

children.solution_md: Use s = ½gt² with t = 2.5 s.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The stone released in the table is let fall for 3.0 s. Use v² = u² + 2as and the depth in the table to find its speed on reaching that depth.

questions.stem_md: A ball is thrown straight up. Compare the time it takes to rise to its highest point with the time it takes to fall back to the point of release, and state the value of g you use.

answer.model_answer_md: Both times are equal. The ball loses $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ every second on the way up and gains the same amount on the way down, so it returns to the hand with the speed it started with. Here $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downward, taken as $-9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ when up is positive.

questions.solution_md: Same acceleration up and down, so equal times.

marking_scheme.step: Times are equal, with the reason

questions.stem_md: A truck driver brakes twice with the same retardation, first at 36 km/h and then at 72 km/h. Compare the braking distances and explain your answer using an equation of motion.

answer.model_answer_md: From $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$, $s = u^2/(2a)$. Doubling the speed from 10 to $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ multiplies $u^2$ by 4, so the braking distance at 72 km/h is four times that at 36 km/h.

questions.solution_md: s ∝ u² for fixed a, so doubling u gives four times the distance.

marking_scheme.step: Braking distance is proportional to the square of the speed

questions.stem_md: A scooter moving at 6 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² for 8 s. Find its final speed and the distance covered, and show that the distance equals average velocity times time.

answer.model_answer_md: The final speed comes from the first equation: $v = u + at = 6 + 1.5(8) = 18\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. answer.model_answer_md: In one revolution the body covers the circumference $2\pi r$ in time $T$. Speed is distance divided by time, so $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$. answer.model_answer_md: Uniform circular motion is motion in a circle at constant speed, like a satellite in a circular orbit or a merry-go-round turning steadily. In one revolution the body covers the circumference $2\pi r$ in one period $T$. Since speed is distance divided by time, its speed is $v = 2\pi r / T$. For the satellite, we substitute the radius and the period in metres and seconds: $v = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14 \times 7.2 \times 10^{6}}{6.0 \times 10^{3}} = 7.54 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, which is about $7.5\ \text{km s}^{-1}$.
